# Introduction

Basketball players have traditionally been described by five positions, yet game-related statistics only partly separate these positions [@sampaio2006discriminant], and a growing literature replaces them with data-driven functional roles [@kalman2020lineup; @ibanez2025redefining; @chen2023modeling; @wei2025enhancing; @pendolareinecke2025exploring]. A recent systematic review identified a set of recurrent roles but concluded that differences between studies largely reflect methodological heterogeneity and called for a unified, high-quality approach [@ribes2026identifying]. Two issues stand out. First, the number of roles is usually chosen with internal validity indices [@duman2021cluster], while the stability of the resulting partition under resampling [@hennig2007cluster] is seldom reported. Second, roles are frequently linked to team or lineup success [@kalman2020lineup; @chen2023modeling; @wei2025enhancing], but lineup outcomes are noisy, lineups are short-lived, and their observations are not independent, so that apparent role effects may reflect the quality of the players involved rather than how their roles combine [@petridis2026lineup; @grassetti2020extended].

Most of this evidence comes from the NBA and from national leagues; for the EuroLeague, lineup-level work has focused on plus-minus modelling [@grassetti2020extended] rather than on roles. The purpose of this study was therefore (1) to derive functional player roles for the EuroLeague from open data with the number of roles determined by cluster stability, (2) to quantify how far these roles cut across registered positions, and (3) to test whether the role composition of a lineup explains its performance beyond the individual quality of its players.
